strategy.method: Alternating series test followed by an absolute-convergence test
strategy.why_this_method: The signs alternate and the magnitude 1/n is positive, decreasing, and approaches zero.
strategy.alternatives: The ratio and root tests are inconclusive because their limits equal 1.

steps.title: Separate the alternating sign from the magnitude
steps.explanation: Write the terms as an alternating sign times a positive magnitude. The test asks whether these magnitudes decrease to zero.
steps.common_mistake: The divergence test alone cannot prove that a series converges.

steps.title: Check that the magnitudes decrease
steps.explanation: As n grows, the positive denominator grows. Therefore the term magnitudes decrease.

steps.title: Check the limiting magnitude
steps.explanation: The second condition is satisfied because the magnitudes vanish. The alternating series therefore converges.

steps.title: Test absolute convergence
steps.explanation: Removing the signs gives the harmonic series. It is a p-series with p = 1, so it diverges.
steps.common_mistake: Convergence of the alternating series does not imply absolute convergence.

final_answer.domain_notes: It converges by alternation but not absolutely.

check.method: compared partial sums with the known alternating harmonic series
check.detail: The partial sums settle while the absolute-value series is harmonic and diverges.

hints: Look separately at the signs and at the magnitude 1/n.
Check the two alternating-series conditions, then test absolute values.
The absolute-value series is the harmonic series.
